topic.title: Changing recurring decimals to fractions
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: M8 Paper 1 only (non-calculator, 75 minutes, 50 marks), usually between Q7 and Q12, and set in most series. A single conversion is 2 marks, M1 for the decimal named and multiplied and A1 for the fraction (Summer 2019 Q8, 0.561 recurring; November 2025 Q10, 0.70 recurring, which 70% completed, many without working). A decimal with a digit outside the block, or a longer block, runs to 3 marks (Summer 2021 Q11, November 2022 Q8, Summer 2022 Q12, November 2023 Q10). Two decimals converted and then subtracted is 4 marks, with follow-through from a candidate's own conversions (Summer 2025 Q12). The schemes accept either route for a digit outside the block: 10x and 100x subtracted, or 10x − x with a decimal that ends on the right, cleared by 10 (9x = 7.3 in Summer 2025; 99x = 8.5 in November 2021).
mustMemorise: Let x be the decimal, multiply by 10 to the power of the block length, subtract, divide, simplify
One power of ten for each digit in the repeating block
A digit before the block that does not repeat needs a second multiplication: use 10^a and 10^(a+b)
After subtracting, no endless tail may remain on the right; a decimal that ends, such as 8.5, is fine and is cleared by multiplying top and bottom by 10
Clear any decimal left in a fraction by multiplying top and bottom by ten
Finish in lowest terms, because that is what the answer line asks for
Every recurring decimal is rational, which is the significance the Teacher Guidance asks about
notOnThisSpec: Infinite-series or limit arguments for the value of a recurring decimal
Proving that a number is irrational
Deciding whether a given number is rational or irrational, which belongs to M8-NA-01 and is a separate topic here
Recurring decimals with a repeating block longer than three digits, which the corpus never sets

note.title: Changing recurring decimals to fractions
note.subject: maths

given: Nothing: no part of this topic appears on the Higher formula sheet
mustKnow: Let x be the decimal, then subtract two multiples of x that share the same endless tail
Multiply by 10^b where b is the number of digits in the repeating block
With a digits before the block, use 10^a and 10^(a+b) and subtract those two
Clear any decimal left in the fraction, then give the answer in lowest terms

notOnThisSpec: Deciding rational against irrational, which is M8-NA-01

mustBeAbleTo: Read CCEA's dot notation and say exactly which digits repeat
Choose the multiplier from the length of the repeating block
Set out the two lines so the endless tails are identical, then subtract them
Handle a decimal with one or more digits before the repeating block by multiplying twice
Clear a decimal that ends, left on the right after subtracting, by multiplying top and bottom by ten
Simplify the resulting fraction to its lowest terms
Convert two recurring decimals and then add, subtract or multiply them exactly
Explain why every recurring decimal is rational
sheet.howExamined: M8 Paper 1 only (non-calculator, 75 minutes, 50 marks), usually between Q7 and Q12, and set in most series. A single conversion is 2 marks, M1 for the decimal named and multiplied and A1 for the fraction (Summer 2019 Q8, 0.561 recurring; November 2025 Q10, 0.70 recurring, which 70% completed, many without working). A decimal with a digit outside the block, or a longer block, runs to 3 marks (Summer 2021 Q11, November 2022 Q8, Summer 2022 Q12, November 2023 Q10). Two decimals converted and then subtracted is 4 marks, with follow-through from a candidate's own conversions (Summer 2025 Q12). The schemes accept either route for a digit outside the block: 10x and 100x subtracted, or 10x − x with a decimal that ends on the right, cleared by 10 (9x = 7.3 in Summer 2025; 99x = 8.5 in November 2021).
traps: Converting only the easier decimal: most candidates gained a mark for the straightforward one, and a reasonable number converted both and subtracted for all four marks (Summer 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q12)
A bare answer: 70% converted the decimal correctly and many showed no working at all (November 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q10); with no working, one slip loses every mark
Treating a digit outside the block as repeating, so 0.83 recurring on the 3 becomes 83/99 instead of 5/6
A multiplier that does not match the block length: the subtraction then leaves a tail that still goes on
Mistaking a decimal that ends for an error: 9x = 7.3 is the scheme's own line; multiply top and bottom by 10
Writing the denominator as 10, 100 or 1000 instead of the 9, 99, 90 or 990 the subtraction leaves
Stopping at a correct fraction that is not in its lowest terms when the question asks for them
Rounding or truncating the decimal and converting that instead: examiners recorded one and often two penalties for inexact decimals carried through (Summer 2023 M3 Q19)

noteBlocks.lede: A third is $0.333\ldots$, going on for ever, and it is still an ordinary fraction. Every recurring decimal is. A short method finds exactly which fraction, with one subtraction that makes the endless tail disappear.
can: Read the dot notation and say which digits repeat.
Choose the multipliers from the digits before and inside the block.
Subtract, clear any decimal, and simplify the fraction.

noteBlocks.text: 1. Two numbers with the same tail

noteBlocks.md: You cannot write $0.\dot{4}$ out in full, and rounding it throws the exactness away. The way round is to make a second number with exactly the same endless tail, then subtract. Call the decimal $x$. Multiplying by 10 moves every digit one place left, and because every digit is a 4, the tail of $10x$ is the tail of $x$.

noteBlocks.alt: Two rows of working lined up at the decimal point: x = 0.4444444… and 10x = 4.4444444…, with the digits after the point shaded to show they are identical. Under a rule, 9x = 4, so x = 4/9.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 118" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Two lines with the same tail"><title>Two lines with the same tail</title><rect x="200" y="19" width="160" height="21" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.1" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="0"/><text x="118" y="34" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">x =</text><text x="196" y="34" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">0</text><text x="196" y="34" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start">.4444444…</text><rect x="200" y="51" width="160" height="21" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.1" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="0"/><text x="118" y="66" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">10x =</text><text x="196" y="66" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">4</text><text x="196" y="66" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start">.4444444…</text><path d="M40 78 L360 78" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><text x="118" y="104" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start" font-weight="600">9x = 4, so x = 4/9</text></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: The tails match digit for digit, so subtracting removes them and leaves whole numbers.

noteBlocks.title: Why the tails cancel
noteBlocks.md: Both lines carry the same digits for ever after the point, so taking one from the other cancels every one of them. Nothing is rounded, which is why the fraction is exact, not an approximation.

noteBlocks.stem: Change the recurring decimal $0.\dot{4}$ to a fraction.

steps.decision: Naming the decimal lets you make a second copy of it. This line is the first thing the scheme looks for.
One digit repeats, so multiply by 10: the point moves one place and the tails line up.
Subtract. Every 4 after the point cancels, and whole numbers are left on both sides.
Divide by 9. It is already in its lowest terms.

noteBlocks.title: Recurring decimals to fractions - Corbettmaths
noteBlocks.why: Corbettmaths 96 works the same four lines on several decimals, including one with a digit that does not repeat. Watch it, then do the question below without scrolling back.

noteBlocks.prompt: Change $0.\dot{8}$ to a fraction in its simplest form.
noteBlocks.explain: As in steps 2 to 4 of See it: $10x = 8.888\ldots$, subtract $x$ and $9x = 8$, so $x = \dfrac{8}{9}$. The 9 comes from the subtraction, not from place value.

twin.prompt: Change $1.\dot{4}$ to a fraction in its simplest form.
twin.explain: $x = 1.444\ldots$ and $10x = 14.444\ldots$, so $9x = 13$ and $x = \dfrac{13}{9}$. A whole-number part changes nothing in the method.

noteBlocks.md: In $0.\dot{3}\dot{6}$ the dots mark the first and last digits of the block, so 36 repeats: $0.363636\ldots$ Multiplying by 10 would shift it half a block, and the tails would not match. Use one power of ten for each digit in the block: 100 for two digits, 1000 for three. Then the subtraction leaves 99 or 999 on the left.

noteBlocks.alt: Two rows lined up at the decimal point: x = 0.3636363… and 100x = 36.3636363…, the matching tails shaded. Under a rule, 99x = 36, so x = 36/99 = 4/11.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 118" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="A two-digit block"><title>A two-digit block</title><rect x="200" y="19" width="160" height="21" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.1" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="0"/><text x="118" y="34" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">x =</text><text x="196" y="34" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">0</text><text x="196" y="34" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start">.3636363…</text><rect x="200" y="51" width="160" height="21" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.1" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="0"/><text x="118" y="66" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">100x =</text><text x="196" y="66" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">36</text><text x="196" y="66" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start">.3636363…</text><path d="M40 78 L360 78" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><text x="118" y="104" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start" font-weight="600">99x = 36, so x = 36/99 = 4/11</text></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: A two-digit block needs 100: the point moves one whole block and the tails line up again.

noteBlocks.stem: Change the recurring decimal $0.\dot{3}\dot{6}$ to a fraction in its simplest form.

steps.decision: Two digits sit under the dots, so the block is 36.
Two digits in the block, so two places: multiply by 100.
The tails cancel, leaving whole numbers.
Divide top and bottom by 9: the last mark is for the lowest terms.

noteBlocks.prompt: Fill the gap: you multiply by one power of ten for each digit in the ______ block.
noteBlocks.answer: repeating | recurring | repeating block | recurring block
noteBlocks.explain: Step 2 of See it: count the digits under the dots and use that many tens. Two digits meant 100; three would mean 1000.

twin.prompt: Fill the gap: a block of three digits needs a multiplier of ______.
twin.explain: One power of ten per digit in the block: three digits, 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000.

noteBlocks.prompt: The decimal $0.\dot{2}4\dot{3}$ has a repeating block of three digits. What do you multiply $x$ by?
noteBlocks.explain: Step 2 of See it, one digit longer: three digits in the block, so three places, 1000. The subtraction then leaves $999x$.

twin.prompt: What do you multiply $x$ by for $0.\dot{5}\dot{8}$?
twin.explain: Two digits in the block, so 100: the point moves one whole block and the tails line up.

noteBlocks.text: 3. When a digit does not repeat

noteBlocks.md: In $0.7\dot{2}$ the dot sits over the 2 only, so the 7 happens once and never again. One multiplication cannot line up both. So do two: multiply by 10 to push the 7 past the point, then by 100 to move one block further. Those two lines share a tail; subtract them.

There is a shorter route, and CCEA's schemes use it: subtract $x$ from $10x$ straight away. The right-hand side then ends, as $9x = 6.5$ does. A decimal that ends is not an error; multiply top and bottom by 10.

noteBlocks.alt: Three rows lined up at the decimal point: x = 0.7222222…, 10x = 7.2222222… and 100x = 72.2222222…. The tails of the last two rows are shaded. Under a rule, 90x = 65, so x = 65/90 = 13/18.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 178" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="A digit that does not repeat"><title>A digit that does not repeat</title><text x="200" y="22" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle" font-style="italic">subtract the two shaded rows</text><text x="118" y="62" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">x =</text><text x="196" y="62" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">0</text><text x="196" y="62" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start">.7222222…</text><rect x="200" y="79" width="160" height="21" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.1" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="0"/><text x="118" y="94" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">10x =</text><text x="196" y="94" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">7</text><text x="196" y="94" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start">.2222222…</text><rect x="200" y="111" width="160" height="21" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.1" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="0"/><text x="118" y="126" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">100x =</text><text x="196" y="126" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">72</text><text x="196" y="126" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start">.2222222…</text><path d="M40 138 L360 138" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><text x="118" y="164" font-size="14" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start" font-weight="600">90x = 65, so x = 65/90 = 13/18</text></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: Only the last two rows share a tail, so those are the two to subtract.

noteBlocks.stem: Change the recurring decimal $0.7\dot{2}$ to a fraction in its simplest form.

steps.decision: Only the 2 carries a dot, so the 7 is outside the block. That decision sets everything else.
Multiply by 10 to push the 7 past the point. From here on everything after the point repeats.
One block further: this line and the last now share a tail.
Subtract the pair with matching tails, divide, and simplify by 5.
The same fraction by the other route. A right-hand side that ends is fine: multiply top and bottom by 10.

noteBlocks.prompt: Change $0.4\dot{6}$ to a fraction in its simplest form.
noteBlocks.explain: Steps 2 to 4 of See it: $10x = 4.666\ldots$ and $100x = 46.666\ldots$, so $90x = 42$ and $x = \dfrac{42}{90} = \dfrac{7}{15}$. Treating both digits as repeating would give $\dfrac{46}{99}$.

twin.prompt: Change $0.1\dot{3}$ to a fraction in its simplest form.

noteBlocks.prompt: Working on $0.3\dot{4}$, you subtract $x$ from $10x$ and get $9x = 3.1$. What next?
options: Start again: the multiplier must be wrong
noteBlocks.explain: Step 5 of See it: the right-hand side ends, so the tails did cancel. $x = \dfrac{3.1}{9}$, and multiplying top and bottom by 10 clears the decimal: $\dfrac{31}{90}$.

twin.prompt: Working on $0.0\dot{4}\dot{5}$, you subtract $x$ from $100x$ and get $99x = 4.5$. What next?
options: Start again: the multiplier must be wrong
twin.explain: 4.5 ends, so the tails did cancel. $\dfrac{4.5}{99} = \dfrac{45}{990}$, which simplifies to $\dfrac{1}{22}$.

optionNotes.option: Start again: the multiplier must be wrong
optionNotes.why: The subtraction left a number that ends, so the tails matched. Only a tail that still goes on would mean the multiplier was wrong.
Rounding changes the value: $\dfrac{5}{99}$ is $0.0505\ldots$, not $0.0454\ldots$

optionNotes.option: Start again: the multiplier must be wrong
optionNotes.why: Only an endless tail left on the right means the lines did not match. A decimal that ends, like 3.1, is expected on this route; CCEA's schemes run $9x = 7.3$.
Rounding throws the exactness away: $\dfrac{3}{9}$ is $0.333\ldots$, not the decimal you started with.

noteBlocks.text: 4. A digit before a longer block

noteBlocks.md: The two moves combine. Count the digits between the point and the block, $a$, and the digits in the block, $b$. Multiply by $10^{a}$ and by $10^{a+b}$, and subtract those two lines. In $0.1\dot{3}\dot{6}$, $a = 1$ and $b = 2$, so the lines are $10x$ and $1000x$, and the subtraction leaves $990x$.

noteBlocks.title: The recipe
noteBlocks.md: Let $x$ be the decimal. Multiply by $10^{a}$ and $10^{a+b}$, subtract those two lines, clear any decimal, then simplify. When nothing sits before the block, $a = 0$ and the first line is $x$ itself.

noteBlocks.stem: Change the recurring decimal $0.1\dot{3}\dot{6}$ to a fraction in its simplest form.

steps.working: Let $x = 0.13636\ldots$: one digit before the block, a block of two.
steps.decision: Read the dots: they sit over the 3 and the 6, so the 1 is outside the block.
$10^{a}$ with $a = 1$ pushes the 1 past the point.
$10^{a+b}$ with $a + b = 3$ moves one whole block further.
Subtract the two lines with matching tails, then simplify: 135 and 990 share 45.

noteBlocks.prompt: Change $0.2\dot{1}\dot{8}$ to a fraction in its simplest form.
noteBlocks.explain: As in See it: $1000x = 218.1818\ldots$ and $10x = 2.1818\ldots$, so $990x = 216$ and $x = \dfrac{216}{990} = \dfrac{12}{55}$. The 990 is the sign that both moves were used.

twin.prompt: Change $0.3\dot{4}\dot{5}$ to a fraction in its simplest form.

noteBlocks.md: CCEA sets this on the non-calculator paper, and it varies more than the decimal. Twists: **two decimals combined**, converted to fractions first and then added or subtracted exactly; **show that** a decimal equals a given fraction, where the working is the mark; and a **bare answer**, which risks every mark if one digit slips.

noteBlocks.title: Examiners' view
noteBlocks.md: Most candidates gained a mark for the easier of two recurring decimals, and a reasonable number converted both and subtracted for all four marks. A minority subtracted the decimals first and then converted, sometimes correctly.

noteBlocks.stem: Work out $0.7\dot{3} - 0.\dot{5}$, giving your answer as a fraction in its lowest terms.

steps.decision: Convert the harder one with both moves; the 7 is outside the block.
The easier one, one move. Use a new letter so the two do not get mixed.
A common denominator of 45, then subtract. It is already in lowest terms.
Subtracting first and converting after gives the same answer: a check, or a route of its own.

noteBlocks.prompt: Work out $0.2\dot{6} + 0.\dot{4}$ as a fraction in its lowest terms.
noteBlocks.explain: As in steps 1 to 3 of See it: $0.2\dot{6} = \dfrac{24}{90} = \dfrac{4}{15}$ and $0.\dot{4} = \dfrac{4}{9}$. Then $\dfrac{12}{45} + \dfrac{20}{45} = \dfrac{32}{45}$.

twin.prompt: Work out $0.\dot{5}\dot{4} - 0.\dot{3}$ as a fraction in its lowest terms.

noteBlocks.text: 6. Why every recurring decimal is a fraction

noteBlocks.md: The method never fails on a recurring decimal, and that is the point of it: it proves every recurring decimal is **rational**, one whole number divided by another. A decimal that neither ends nor repeats, like the one for $\sqrt{2}$, never lines up with a copy of itself, and that is what makes it irrational.

noteBlocks.title: Not on this specification
noteBlocks.md: Infinite-series or limit arguments, and proving that a number is irrational. Deciding whether a given number is rational belongs to the surds statement, M8-NA-01, a separate topic here.

noteBlocks.stem: Explain why any recurring decimal can be written as a fraction.

steps.working: Let $x$ be the decimal, with $a$ digits before its repeating block and $b$ digits in it.
steps.decision: Every recurring decimal fits this description, whatever its digits.
The second is the first moved one whole block along.

steps.working: Subtracting leaves $(10^{a+b} - 10^{a})x$ equal to a number that ends.
steps.decision: The tails cancel exactly; nothing is rounded.

steps.working: Clearing any decimal, $x$ is one whole number divided by another.
steps.decision: That is the definition of a rational number.

noteBlocks.prompt: Why does this method prove that every recurring decimal is rational?
options: Because it always ends with x equal to one whole number divided by another
Because a recurring decimal can be rounded to a fraction
Because every decimal, recurring or not, is rational
noteBlocks.answer: Because it always ends with x equal to one whole number divided by another
noteBlocks.explain: Steps 3 and 4 of See it: the subtraction always leaves whole numbers once any decimal is cleared, so $x$ is one integer over another. That is what rational means.

optionNotes.option: Because a recurring decimal can be rounded to a fraction
optionNotes.why: Rounding gives a fraction close to the decimal, not equal to it. Rational means exactly one whole number over another.

optionNotes.option: Because every decimal, recurring or not, is rational
optionNotes.why: A decimal that never ends and never repeats, like the one for $\sqrt{2}$, is irrational: without a repeat there is no copy to subtract.

twin.prompt: Which decimal can the subtraction method NOT turn into a fraction?
options: One that never ends and never repeats, such as 0.1010010001…
twin.answer: One that never ends and never repeats, such as 0.1010010001…
twin.explain: With no repeating block there is no power of ten that lines a copy up with it, so the tail never cancels.

optionNotes.why: Its block 10 repeats: $100x - x = 99x = 10$, so it is $\dfrac{10}{99}$.
Two digits sit before the block: $1000x - 100x = 900x = 111$, so it is $\dfrac{111}{900}$.

noteBlocks.md:
Read the dot notation and say which digits repeat.
Multiply by $10^{a}$ and $10^{a+b}$, and subtract the lines whose tails match.
Clear a decimal that ends by multiplying top and bottom by 10.
Give the fraction in its lowest terms, and combine two decimals as fractions.

Two to four marks on the non-calculator paper. The first mark is for naming the decimal and the multiplied line; the last is for the fraction in its lowest terms. Two decimals combined is four marks, with follow-through from your own conversions. Stuck: write x equal to the decimal and multiply by the power of ten that moves one whole block.

steps.decision: Naming the decimal is what makes the subtraction possible. Nothing has been calculated yet, but this line is the one the scheme looks for first.

options: So that two multiples of the same number can be subtracted from each other
So that the decimal can be rounded to three places
Because every fraction question has to start with a letter
whyMenu.explain: The whole method is a subtraction of two numbers with identical endless tails. That is only possible if both are multiples of the same $x$.

steps.decision: The repeating block is 2 digits long, so multiplying by 100 moves the decimal point exactly one whole block. The digits after the point are now identical to those in line 1.
The tails are the same, so they cancel exactly and a whole number is left. This is the step the endless decimal is defeated by.
Divide, then simplify. The question asked for the simplest form, so 45/99 on its own would not be finished.

steps.working: Let $x = 0.16666666...$. The 1 does not repeat; only the 6 does.
steps.decision: Deciding which digits repeat is the decision the whole question turns on. A dot sits over the 6 alone, so the 1 is outside the block.
Multiplying by 10 pushes the non-repeating digit past the decimal point. From here on, everything after the point repeats.
One more block along. Lines 2 and 3 now have identical tails, so those two are the pair to subtract; line 1 is not used again.
Subtract, divide, simplify. A denominator of 90 rather than 99 is the sign that the two-multiplication route was used.

items.stem: To change $0.\dot{6}\dot{2}$ to a fraction you let $x = 0.6262\ldots$. What do you multiply $x$ by?
items.skill: Match the multiplier to the length of the repeating block

options.feedback: The block 62 is 2 digits long, so multiplying by 100 moves the point one whole block and the tails line up.
10 moves the point half a block here, so the tails do not match and the subtraction leaves a tail that goes on.
That moves the point one and a half blocks. One power of ten per digit in the block: 2 digits means 100.

items.skill: Read a two-digit block that starts with 0

options.feedback: The block is 07, two digits: $100x - x = 99x = 7$.
That is $0.07$, which stops. The subtraction leaves $99x$, not a power of ten.
$\dfrac{7}{9}$ is $0.777\ldots$. Both dots mark the block 07, so it is two digits long.

items.stem: For $x = 0.5\dot{2}$, which two lines have identical tails after the point?
items.skill: Two multiplications when a digit does not repeat

options.feedback: $10x = 5.222\ldots$ and $100x = 52.222\ldots$ both have only 2s after the point; subtracting leaves $90x = 47$.
$x = 0.5222\ldots$ still has the 5 that never comes back, while $100x = 52.222\ldots$ has only 2s after the point.
$10x = 5.222\ldots$ has only 2s after the point, but $x$ still starts with its 5.

items.stem: A correct method gives $99x = 42$. What is the final answer?

options.feedback: Divide top and bottom by 3: 42/99 = 14/33.
The value is right, but the answer asks for the simplest form: 42 and 99 share 3.
The denominator comes from the subtraction, 99, not from place value.

items.stem: What is $0.9\dot{4}$ as a fraction in its simplest form?
items.skill: A digit outside the block, then simplify

options.feedback: Right value, not yet simplified: divide top and bottom by 5.
Both digits were treated as repeating. Only the 4 carries a dot.
That is 0.94, which stops. The decimal goes on, so the value is a little larger.

items.stem: Which of these is exactly equal to $0.\dot{1}\dot{2}$?

options.feedback: That is 0.12, which stops: rounding the decimal gives a nearby fraction, not an equal one.
A two-digit block leaves 99x, and 12/9 is more than 1.
1/8 is 0.125, which stops. The decimal here is 0.1212…

items.stem: Prerequisite, from fractions and decimals. Which fraction is equal to 0.35?

options.feedback: 0.35 is 35 hundredths, and 35/100 simplifies by 5 to 7/20.
35/10 is 3.5. Two decimal places means hundredths.
3/5 is 0.6. The digits 3 and 5 are not a numerator and a denominator.

items.stem: Prerequisite, from fractions. Write $\dfrac{54}{90}$ in its lowest terms.

options.feedback: Right value, but 6 and 10 still share 2.
Divided by 2 only; 27 and 45 still share 9.

items.skill: Add fractions with a common denominator

options.feedback: Tops and bottoms were added separately. Put both over a common denominator first.
The numerators were added over the product of the denominators, but each numerator must be scaled first: 1/6 = 9/54 and 2/9 = 12/54.

context.setting: A recurring decimal to be written as a fraction

parts.stem: Change the recurring decimal $0.\dot{3}$ to a fraction in its simplest form.
hints: The repeating block is 1 digit long, so multiply by 10.
Subtract the two lines: the endless tails are identical, so they cancel.

context.setting: A recurring decimal to be written as a fraction

parts.stem: Change the recurring decimal $0.\dot{7}$ to a fraction in its simplest form.
hints: The repeating block is 1 digit long, so multiply by 10.
Subtract the two lines: the endless tails are identical, so they cancel.
parts.workedSolution: Let $x = 0.77777777...$. Then $10x = 7.7777777...$, and subtracting gives $9x = 7$, so $x = 7/9$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the terminating decimal $0.7$. The denominator comes from the subtraction, which leaves $9x = 7$.

context.setting: A recurring decimal to be written as a fraction

parts.stem: Change the recurring decimal $0.\dot{2}\dot{7}$ to a fraction in its simplest form.
hints: The repeating block is 2 digits long, so multiply by 100.
Subtract the two lines: the endless tails are identical, so they cancel.

commonErrors.feedback: A multiplier of $10$ leaves a recurring tail on both sides, so the subtraction does not clear it. The block is 2 digits, so multiply by 100 and the answer is $3/11$.
The value is right. If you wrote $27/99$ and stopped, the method marks stand but the final mark asks for the simplest form: divide by 9.

context.setting: A recurring decimal to be written as a fraction

parts.stem: Change the recurring decimal $0.\dot{1}3\dot{5}$ to a fraction in its simplest form.
hints: The repeating block is 3 digits long, so multiply by 1000.
Subtract the two lines: the endless tails are identical, so they cancel.

context.setting: A recurring decimal to be written as a fraction

parts.stem: Change the recurring decimal $0.8\dot{3}$ to a fraction in its simplest form.
hints: One digit here does not repeat, so you need two multiplications before you subtract.
Subtract the two lines: the endless tails are identical, so they cancel.
parts.workedSolution: Let $x = 0.83333333...$. Then $10x = 8.33333333...$ and $100x = 83.3333333...$. Subtracting the first of these from the second, $90x = 75$, so $x = 75/90 = 5/6$.

commonErrors.feedback: Both digits have been treated as repeating. Only the 3 carries a dot, so multiply by 10 first and then by 100, which leaves $90x$.

emphasis: a zero before the repeating block

context.setting: A recurring decimal to be written as a fraction

parts.stem: Change the recurring decimal $0.0\dot{2}$ to a fraction in its simplest form.
hints: One digit here does not repeat, so you need two multiplications before you subtract.
Subtract the two lines: the endless tails are identical, so they cancel.
A zero counts as a non-repeating digit like any other.
parts.workedSolution: Let $x = 0.02222222...$. Then $10x = 0.22222222...$ and $100x = 2.2222222...$. Subtracting the first of these from the second, $90x = 2$, so $x = 2/90 = 1/45$.

emphasis: one non-repeating digit and a two-digit block

context.setting: A recurring decimal to be written as a fraction

parts.stem: Change the recurring decimal $0.4\dot{1}\dot{6}$ to a fraction in its simplest form.
hints: One digit here does not repeat, so you need two multiplications before you subtract.
Subtract the two lines: the endless tails are identical, so they cancel.

context.setting: A printed result about a recurring decimal

hints: Use the same method as any other one-digit recurring decimal.
Do not stop because the answer looks surprising: follow the algebra.
parts.workedSolution: Let $x = 0.99999999...$. Then $10x = 9.9999999...$, and subtracting gives $9x = 9$, so $x = 9/9 = 1$. The two are two spellings of the same number, not two numbers that are nearly equal.

context.setting: A product of two recurring decimals

parts.stem:
Work out the value of $0.\dot{1}\dot{8} \times 0.\dot{7}$.

Give your answer as a fraction in its lowest terms.
hints: Convert each decimal on its own first; multiplying the decimals is not possible by hand.
$0.\dot{1}\dot{8}$ has a two-digit block: $99x = 18$.
Multiply the numerators and the denominators, then cancel.
parts.workedSolution: $0.\dot{1}\dot{8}$: $100x - x = 99x = 18$, so it is $\dfrac{18}{99} = \dfrac{2}{11}$. $0.\dot{7}$: $9y = 7$, so it is $\dfrac{7}{9}$. The product is $\dfrac{2}{11} \times \dfrac{7}{9} = \dfrac{14}{99}$.

commonErrors.feedback: Rounding each decimal first and multiplying gives a number close to the answer but not equal to it. Convert both to fractions and the multiplication is exact.
The two-digit block was divided by 9, which treats it as one digit. $99x = 18$ for $0.\dot{1}\dot{8}$, so it is $\dfrac{2}{11}$.

questions.solutionProgram: 0.18rec = 18/99 = 2/11; 0.7rec = 7/9; product 14/99; 18/9 x 7/9 = 14/9 when the block is treated as one digit

context.setting: A recurring decimal to be written as a fraction

parts.stem: Change the recurring decimal $0.\dot{5}\dot{1}$ to a fraction in its simplest form.
hints: The repeating block is 2 digits long, so multiply by 100.
Subtract the two lines: the endless tails are identical, so they cancel.

emphasis: two conversions, one of them with a non-repeating digit

context.setting: A sum of two recurring decimals

parts.stem:
Work out the value of $0.\dot{1} + 0.0\dot{5}$.

Give your answer as a fraction in its lowest terms.

scheme.for: $10x - x$ used for the first decimal, or $1/9$ seen

scheme.examinerNote: Follow through from either conversion. A candidate's two fractions correctly added and simplified earn this mark.

hints: Convert each decimal separately. The second one has a digit that does not repeat.
Write both fractions over a denominator of 18, since 9 and 18 both divide into it.
Simplify at the very end, once, rather than part-way through.
parts.workedSolution:
First decimal: $10x - x = 9x = 1$, so $0.\dot{1} = 1/9$.

Second decimal: $100x - 10x = 90x = 5$, so $0.0\dot{5} = 5/90 = 1/18$.

Adding over a denominator of 18: $\dfrac{1}{9} = \dfrac{2}{18}$, so the sum is $\dfrac{2}{18} + \dfrac{1}{18} = \dfrac{3}{18}$, and dividing top and bottom by 3 gives $\dfrac{1}{6}$.

commonErrors.feedback: The first conversion is right and its marks stand. In the second, both digits were treated as repeating, which gives $5/99$. Only the 5 carries a dot, so the subtraction leaves $90x = 5$ and the value is $1/18$.
Both conversions and the addition are correct, so three marks stand. The last mark is for the simplest form: $3/18$ still has a common factor of 3, and dividing it out gives $1/6$.

parts.stem: Change the recurring decimal $0.2\dot{7}$ to a fraction in its simplest form.
hints: Only the 7 carries a dot, so the 2 does not repeat.
Multiply by 10, then by 100, and subtract those two lines.

commonErrors.feedback: Both digits were treated as repeating, which gives $\dfrac{27}{99}$. Only the 7 carries a dot: multiply by 10 and by 100, and $90x = 25$.
$\dfrac{27}{100}$ is $0.27$, which stops. The subtraction leaves $90x = 25$, so the denominator comes from 90, not from place value.

parts.stem: Hence work out $0.2\dot{7} + 0.\dot{2}$, giving your answer as a fraction in its lowest terms.

scheme.for: $\dfrac{1}{2}$ (follow through their part (a) plus $\dfrac{2}{9}$, in lowest terms)

hints: $0.\dot{2}$ is one digit repeating: $9y = 2$.
parts.workedSolution: $0.\dot{2} = \dfrac{2}{9} = \dfrac{4}{18}$, so the sum is $\dfrac{5}{18} + \dfrac{4}{18} = \dfrac{9}{18}$, which is $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

commonErrors.feedback: The value is right; the last mark asks for the lowest terms, and nine eighteenths is one half.

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh was asked to change $0.3\dot{2}$ to a fraction in its simplest form. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 reads the dot notation wrongly. The dot sits over the 2 only, so the decimal is $0.32222\ldots$, not $0.3232\ldots$. Everything after that line is careful work on the wrong number.
findTheMistake.feedback: The method is sound, and it is worked on the wrong decimal. One dot means one repeating digit; two dots mark the first and last digits of the block. Here only the 2 repeats, so multiply by 10 and 100: $90x = 29$.

findTheMistake.stem: Ciarán was asked to change $0.\dot{4}\dot{1}$ to a fraction in its simplest form. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 multiplies by 10, half a block for the two-digit block 41. The tails of $x$ and $10x$ do not match, so line 3 is really $3.7272\ldots$, a decimal that still goes on, and cutting it to 3.73 makes the answer wrong.
findTheMistake.feedback: Naming the decimal earns the first mark. Then use one power of ten per digit in the block: two digits, so 100. After the subtraction no endless tail may be left on the right.

prompts.prompt: A repeating block has b digits. What do you multiply by?
prompts.answer: 10 to the power b: one power of ten per repeating digit.

prompts.prompt: After subtracting you get 9x = 6.5. Is the multiplier wrong?
prompts.answer: No: a decimal that ends is fine; multiply top and bottom by 10.

prompts.prompt: Why is every recurring decimal rational?
prompts.answer: The subtraction always leaves whole numbers, so it is one integer over another.

prompts.prompt: Your subtraction gives 33/99. Is that the answer?
prompts.answer: Not yet: simplify to lowest terms, 1/3.

prompts.prompt: A digit sits before the block. How many multiplications do you need?
prompts.answer: Two: one moves that digit past the point, one more moves a whole block.
